credits.readme:
*Les Roses: Rosa Lucida*, P. J. Redouté pinx., Bessin sculp., Imprimerie de Rémond,
1817-24, stipple and line engraving printed in colour and finished by hand. The
Cleveland Museum of Art, Mr. and Mrs. Charles G. Prasse Collection, 1965.290, Open Access
(CC0). The separation into print and watercolour, the dots, and the maps are ours. No
third-party code.

files.text:
Pierre-Joseph Redouté came to Paris from the Ardennes with almost nothing, a painter’s son who had spent his teens going from town to town painting portraits and altarpieces, and found work drawing the flowers of the Jardin du Roi. He drew them for Marie-Antoinette, and after the Revolution, which he survived by being useful, for the Muséum. Then for Joséphine Bonaparte, who in 1799 bought the house at Malmaison and filled its gardens and glasshouses with plants from everywhere. For her he made the eight volumes of Les Liliacées, lilies and irises and amaryllis, nearly five hundred plates.

Les Roses came after her. Joséphine died at Malmaison in May 1814, and the first part of the book appeared three years later, 168 plates in thirty parts, with a text by the botanist Claude-Antoine Thory. It is often called the roses of Malmaison, but most of them were drawn in the nurseries and gardens of Paris and its suburbs; this one, Rosa lucida, the shining rose, is a wild rose of the American north-east, named for the gloss on its leaves.

Redouté did not engrave. He painted each rose in watercolour on vellum, and the paintings went to engravers, here a man called Bessin, others Langlois, Chapuy, Victor, Charlin, who cut them into copper not in lines but in dots, tens of thousands to a plate. The printing was done by Rémond, and the way it was done is the reason a printed page of Redouté can be mistaken for a painting.

Stipple was a London fashion when Redouté first saw it. The engraver laid an etching ground on polished copper and pricked the drawing through it with needles and a toothed wheel, the dots set close where the shade was deep and loose where the petal turned to the light, then let acid bite them; afterwards he went over the plate with a curved graver for the palest tones, which acid could not make fine enough. Contours were dots too, or the faintest line. Nothing on the plate says where a petal stops. The eye does that, from how the dots crowd and thin.

The printer inked it à la poupée, with a dolly of rolled rag for each colour: rose madder into the flowers, green into the leaves, yellow into the stamens, black into the lettering, each worked into its own few square inches of copper and a little past them. Then the warm plate was wiped with stiff muslin and finished with the palm of the hand until the surface shone, the colours left only down in the dots, and a sheet of dampened paper went through the press on top of it. One pull, every colour at once. The damp paper drew the ink up out of each pit and it spread a fraction as it landed, so the dots softened into one another; that is the bloom on a Redouté petal, which no line engraving can give.

The print that comes off the plate is pale and a little flat, the colour of a pressed flower. Colourists finished each impression by hand, laying transparent watercolour over the printed colour, glaze on glaze in the cup of each flower, a warmer green on the lit side of the leaves, the red of the hip, a touch of something brighter in the stamens. No two copies of the book are quite alike, and the best of them were taken for paintings by people who should have known better.

# stipple-rose A plate from Redouté's *Les Roses* (Paris, 1817-24), *Rosa lucida*, made in front of you as you scroll, in the order it was really made. It opens close up on the engraved copper: tens of thousands of tiny pits in polished metal, the rose the wrong way round, lit from one side so each pit shows a bright wall and a dark one. The view pulls back to the whole plate. Then it is inked à la poupée: rose madder dabbed into the flowers with a rag dolly in soft round dabs a little past the petals, green over the foliage, yellow into the stamens, black into the lettering, each colour wiped off the surface behind the dolly in curved tarlatan strokes, so the colour stays only down in the dots with a faint plate tone left on the copper. The dampened sheet is laid on from its lower edge and lowered over a bend, the press passes down it once as a travelling band of compression (the image shows through the damp sheet and the plate's edge is pressed into it), and the sheet is peeled back from its left edge and turned over to the right, beside the plate: the print, the right way round, pale and flat. Last, the colourist's watercolour: the leaves greened passage by passage, the hip, the bud, the flowers glazed petal by petal from the base outward, the stamens, and the deep flush of the petals laid last and slowest. Wet glaze is darker and glossy and dries lighter and matte, with pigment at the rim and settled in the tooth. The last frame is the scan of the real plate, pixel for pixel. Scroll back and it all un-makes. ```html
``` Or `import { stippleRose } from './stipple-rose.js'` and call `stippleRose(section, { src, mode, runway, webgl })`; it returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | what it does | |---------------|----------|----------|--------------| | `data-src` | `src` | required | The plate's JSON (sizes, the poupée groups with their camera tracks, the wash areas). Beside it: `.webp` (the plate), `-wash.webp` (the watercolour layer as a transmittance, half size), `-paper.webp` (the sheet's own paper, quarter size), `-dots.webp` (lossless: the engraved dots, one byte per 3-source-px cell), `-ink.webp` (lossless: poupée group, dab arrival, wipe, dab edge) and `-wmap.webp` (lossless: wash area, wet-front arrival, distance to edge). | | `data-mode` | `mode` | `scroll` | `scroll`: a pinned stage on a runway. `static`: the finished plate as an image. | | `data-runway` | `runway` | `380` | Section height in svh. The stage is pinned for `runway - 100` svh of travel. | | `data-webgl` | `webgl` | `on` | `off` leaves the finished plate as an image. (WebGL2 is required; without it, the image.) | The timeline, as fractions of the runway (`ST` and `INKWIN` at the top of the JS): the close-up 0-0.115 (held, then pulled back), inking 0.11-0.37 (flowers, hip, leaves, stamens, lettering; each colour's wipe follows its dabs), the paper laid on 0.375-0.426, the press 0.426-0.462, the peel 0.466-0.535, the plate taken away 0.528-0.565, the watercolour 0.565-0.95, then the finished plate. Events (bubbling, for sound later): `stipple-rose:stage` with `detail: { stage }` as each stage begins while scrolling forward (`ink`, `pull`, `press`, `peel`, `finish`), `stipple-rose:dab` with `detail: { group, kind }` as each colour goes on, and `stipple-rose:done` when the last wash is dry. ## The real thing What we read and modelled (dealer and museum notes on *Les Roses* from Shapero, Camille Sourget, Christie's and George Glazer; technique notes on stipple engraving from the Oxford History of Science Museum, Russborough and Elizabeth Harvey-Lee; the Cleveland Museum's record of this impression). Notes in the builder's scratch folder. - **The copper.** Stipple: an etching ground on polished copper, the drawing pricked through it as dots with needles and a roulette, bitten in acid, the ground cleaned off, the palest tones added with the stipple graver. Contours as dots or the faintest line. The plate carries the image mirror-wise. Here the dots are the real dots of this impression, found one by one in the Cleveland Museum's 400 dpi scan, drawn as round (not quite round) pits in copper, each lit from the upper left, with the lit lip of the pit just outside it. Polished copper, a warm orange-brown, reflects a studio window: a crisp bright pane and a crisp dark band across a mid-toned room, their edges wavering a little because a plate is never quite flat. The reflection is fixed to the screen, so it slides over the metal as the plate moves. Fine polishing scratches run one way and catch the window; the margins are tarnished by handling; the narrow bevel catches a bright line on its upper and left sides. A pit scatters light: dark against the bright metal, a little lighter than the dark band, as a real plate does. - **Inking à la poupée.** Stiff inks of several colours on one plate, each worked into its area with a dolly of rolled rag: soft round dabs, landing a little past the area; the warm plate wiped with tarlatan in circles and finished with the palm, so the surface is clean copper and the colour is left in the dots. Here each dab is a disc that spreads from its centre with a ragged edge, thicker in the middle, with a raised lip that catches the light on the side facing it and the print of the rag's weave where the cloth bore down; the film is stiff, tacky and glossy, the window breaking up on its lumps. The wipe follows the dabs in curved strokes (arcs about a point off the plate): the film clears stroke by stroke, and a faint streaked plate tone stays on the copper. - **The pull.** Damp paper laid face down, one pass of the press, the sheet peeled off. Here the sheet's lower edge touches first and the rest is lowered over a bend (the part still in the air foreshortened, lit a little more, a touch larger as it is nearer the eye, shading the plate below it); then a darker band of compression travels down it once with a faint raised wave ahead of it; behind it the image shows faintly through the damp back and the plate mark is pressed in; then the sheet is lifted at its left edge and rolled over a curl to the right. Turned over that way, the printed face is the right way round, so the print is revealed true beside the mirrored plate (the geometry of the turn is exact: the sheet lands where the finished plate stays). - **Hand finishing.** Transparent watercolour over the printed colour. Modelled as in `hand-colouring`: each wash spreads as a wet front from where the brush went down, slowed by the engraved outlines; wet is darker and glossy; drying goes edge first with pigment drawn to the rim and settling in the tooth. The flowers are laid petal by petal (split along the engraved outlines, taken round the flower, each from its base outward) and glazed twice: a first glaze, then the deep flush. Simplified: the press's roller and blankets are not drawn (only its band of compression); the palm's final wipe is not a separate pass; the printer's order of colours and the colourist's order of washes are ours; the poupée areas come from the print's colours, so a dab never strays into a neighbour's colour; the split of the scan into print and watercolour is a reconstruction (below); body-colour highlights are not separated (this scan shows few). ## How it works **Offline (Python, scripts in the builder's scratch folder).** In linear-light optical density, against the sheet's own paper: 1. *The paper.* The engraved area is where the stipple's fine-scale energy is (paper fibres are isolated specks); the paper under it is filled from around it (normalised convolution at growing scales), so the toning of the old sheet stays paper. 2. *Print and watercolour.* `D = Dp + Dw`. Between the dots the paper carries only watercolour, so `Dw` is the floor of the density: a small grey opening (the gaps between dots), then a larger one, which moves everything finer than about 1.5 mm (contours, vein shading, lettering) into the print. `Dp = D - Dw` is the ink on the dots. `paper · exp(-Dp)` is the pull: a pale, flat, grainy colour print. 3. *The dots.* Local peaks of the print layer at full resolution (230,000 of them), with sub-pixel centres, packed one per 3 px cell (4 bits x, 4 bits y). Their size comes, in the shader, from the print's tone where they sit. 4. *Poupée groups.* The print's ink colour (the direction of its density vector): rose, green, yellow, black (lettering). Dab centres are spread over each area, ordered in serpentine bands along its axis; each pixel stores the first dab to reach it and how far it is from that dab's centre; the wipe is the dab order, smoothed, with a swirl. 5. *Wash areas.* The watercolour layer's colour: the flowers (split at the stamens), bud, hip, stamens, the small last touches, and the foliage cut into leaflets along the engraved outlines (watershed) and grouped into ten passages. Arrival is geodesic (scikit-image `MCP_Geometric`) along a brush path, slowed on the print's dark lines; the flowers petal by petal. The petals' first glaze is their density up to its 40th percentile; the flush is the rest. **In the browser.** One quad, one fragment shader (WebGL2). World coordinates are sheet units; the finished sheet is at `[0,1]²` and the plate and paper lie to its left, offset by one sheet width plus half the curl's circumference, so the turned sheet lands exactly on it. The copper draws the print density as a tone when the dots are smaller than a pixel and the real dots, analytically (a 3x3 cell search, anti-aliased by the pixel's footprint), when the view is close; the two blend between 0.75 and 1.5 source px per device px. The watercolour stage computes `O · exp(Dw - D)` where `D` is the washes laid so far (wet looks easing into the real layer as each part dries); when every wash is dry `D = Dw` and the pixel is `O`, the scan. - The plate's picture is resampled to about the size it is shown and mipmapped; the maps go up exact (unpremultiplied ImageBitmaps) and are sampled nearest. - Scroll is followed on a critically damped spring (quicker going back). - Camera (a function of scroll only, smoothed along it): the close-up is about 0.42 source px per device px (6x on desktop, 16x on a phone), held, then pulled back in log space with the point under the glass kept still. On a narrow screen the view zooms in (up to 1.7x) and follows the dolly and the brush; during the peel it keeps the plate and the turned sheet in view and settles on the sheet; it pulls back to the whole sheet before the end. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |---------------|-----------------|----------| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | the page around the plate and the sheet (read from the section's background) | | `--sr-gutter` | `var(--gutter)` | side padding of the stage (the demo uses 5px on phones so the sheet fills the width) | | `--sr-runway` | set by the script | section height in scroll mode | ## Accessibility and motion - Without JS, without WebGL2, or with `data-webgl="off"`, the finished plate is an ``. The canvas is `aria-hidden`. The art is ornament (`alt=""`); credits are in `assets/credits.json`. - Reduced motion: no runway and no canvas, the finished plate, still. If the setting changes mid-visit it settles on the finished plate. - Phone: nothing is interactive, so a swipe always scrolls. ## Cost - Assets 1.8 MB: plate 1.0 MB, dots 0.31 MB, ink map 0.27 MB, wash map 0.16 MB (all three lossless), watercolour 48 KB, paper 8 KB, JSON 8 KB. - One full-screen quad. Most pixels do a handful of texture reads; close up on the copper a pixel reads its 3x3 dot cells. A frame draws only while the scroll spring moves and the section is on screen (IntersectionObserver); nothing runs when the scroll is still, off screen or in a hidden tab. DPR capped at 2. ## Making another plate Scripts in the builder's scratch folder: `s1_split.py` (paper, print and watercolour split, full resolution), `s2_dots.py` and `s2d_grid1.py` (the dots), `s3_layers.py` (output size), `s5_class.py` (ink and wash colours), `s6_groups.py` (poupée groups, dabs, wipe, wash areas, petals, arrival), `s7_export.py`. A plate needs a scan where the stipple is resolved (about 400 dpi); look at the print layer and the wash layer at full size before going on, and at the group maps. ## Credits *Les Roses: Rosa Lucida*, P. J. Redouté pinx., Bessin sculp., Imprimerie de Rémond, 1817-24, stipple and line engraving printed in colour and finished by hand. The Cleveland Museum of Art, Mr. and Mrs. Charles G. Prasse Collection, 1965.290, Open Access (CC0). The separation into print and watercolour, the dots, and the maps are ours. No third-party code.
